data.aac#AAC (since v0.6.0):
AAC is available since decode v0.6.0; v0.5.4 and earlier do not decode it. HE-AAC v2 follows in v0.7.0, with its full profile by default in v0.8.0.
AAC-LC, written in Go from ISO/IEC 14496-3 (mono to 7.1, 8 to 96 kHz; M/S and intensity stereo, perceptual noise substitution, TNS, pulses, short windows), output f32le. Main, LTP, SSR, 960-sample frames, coupling channels and channel configurations 11, 12 and 14 are refused with ErrAudioUnsupported. HE-AAC v1 (SBR over AAC-LC) decodes at twice the core rate, whether the AudioSpecificConfig signals it or the stream only carries it. SBR in its downsampled mode is refused. Gapless: an MP4’s iTunSMPB item and edit lists are applied to AAC as ffmpeg does. DecodeAudioTrack applies it, NewAudioTrack does not. HE-AAC v2 (Parametric Stereo) is supported since v0.7.0, and the full profile is the default since v0.8.0: procedure B for ICC modes 3 to 5, and IPD/OPD with their smoothing and interpolation, as the _ur references of ISO’s vectors are. 34-band streams keep 34 bands (a baseline decoder maps them to 20, so one ISO vector, al_sbr_ps_06, matches its _ur reference but not its baseline one, 2226 LSB off). v0.7.0 mixed with baseline mixing only (procedure A, IPD/OPD ignored). A mono core that signals SBR is announced as stereo from the first frame. Checked: all 7 of 7 ISO PS vectors match the _ur references at 0.033 LSB, and 801 mono PS files of the author’s library are within 1.1e-5 of ffmpeg 9.0.2. Checked: the error against a float64 reference of the same bitstream is about half of ffmpeg’s on the five fixtures; HE-AAC is within 3e-6 of ffmpeg 9.0.2 on four; 12 of the 15 ISO/IEC 14496-26 conformance vectors pass. Speed (go-avkit/decode#35): a decode-only benchmark (BenchmarkAACDecodeReuse, one core) against the median utime of ffmpeg 9.0.2 -threads 1, which is a whole process that also opens and demuxes the file. Go 1.27.4, Apple M4 Max, 10-minute inputs, five interleaved rounds at 1-minute load 6.02 to 6.46:
Input decode (ms) ffmpeg utime (ms) decode / ffmpeg 5.1, 48 kHz 793.4 821 0.966 stereo, 48 kHz 309.0 472 0.655 HE-AAC v2 is slower than ffmpeg on one core: about 1.5 times its utime on an x86 server core and about 1.1 times on an Apple M4, an open defect (go-avkit/decode#77). Since v0.16.1 the SBR filter banks run in float32: 699 ms to 670 ms (-4.2 %) on Zen 4 for a short parametric-stereo clip, 1.59 to 1.52 times ffmpeg; v0.17.1 drives the parametric-stereo all-pass plan by tick (2053 to 2044 us, -0.45 %, marginal), and the whole decode is now measured at 1.42 times ffmpeg’s user time (2026-11-25, Zen 4, one pinned core, load about 1, 9 interleaved rounds, ps4-he2.mp4: decode 643 ms median, ffmpeg 6.1.1 with one thread 453 ms user plus 209 ms system, 659 ms real; the system time is not paid by our in-process benchmark, so user time is the comparable figure; 1.74 when decode#77 opened). Same method, a 620 s HE-AAC v2 file, as measured for v0.8.0 (Go 1.27.4, interleaved rounds, one row per machine; the Zen 4 row below is the v0.16.0 measurement, the M4 row was not repeated):
Machine, date decode / ffmpeg 1-minute load ffmpeg AMD Ryzen 9 7950X (Zen 4), Ubuntu 24.04, 2026-11-15 1.62 (1.60 to 1.65 in three runs) 0.13 to 0.93 6.1.1 Apple M4 Max, 2026-11-15, indicative 1.11 7.0 to 7.7 9.0.2 The two ffmpeg versions differ, so the rows do not compare the machines. The M4 ratio is at a load just under the gate and moves with it (1.37 to 1.47 earlier at a load of 1.6 and 6 to 7). It was 1.74 on the M4 before the speed work of v0.8.0.
Mono was not measured. The README of decode states each of these with its conditions.
data.audio#Audio:
id, _ := decode.FirstAudioTrack(r) pcm, err := decode.DecodeAudioTrack(r, id, decode.AudioConfig{}) for _, a := range pcm { // presentation order, trimmed as the container states use(a.Data, a.Format, a.SampleRate, a.Channels, a.Layout, a.PTS) } NewAudioTrack streams it with DecodeSample and Flush. Data is interleaved little-endian PCM (s16le, s32le or f32le). The start of the track is dropped as its container states it (edit list, Opus pre-skip).
Codec Library Output Checked against ffmpeg FLAC mewkiz/flac s16le up to 16 bits, s32le up to 24 bit-exact on 13 fixtures MP3 (Layer III) tphakala/go-mp3 f32le maximum error 1.07e-6 on 10 fixtures, sample counts equal Opus pion/opus f32le, 48 kHz passes opus_compare on all 12 RFC 8251 test vectors, mono and stereo Linear PCM (WAVE; ipcm, fpcm, raw ), since v0.9.0 this package s16le, s32le or f32le bit-exact on 6 WAVE fixtures (s16, s24, s32, f32, f64, u8); 64-bit float is rounded to f32le, which is lossy Linear PCM takes its width and byte order from the pcmC record of the track’s sample entry; an entry without the record is ErrAudioConfig.
FLAC: 4 to 24 bits, 1 to 8 channels; a 32-bit stream is refused with ErrAudioUnsupported. MP3: MPEG-1, 2 and 2.5, mono and stereo. MP2 (Layer II) is not decoded and is refused with ErrAudioUnsupported. Opus: mono and stereo (mapping family 0); more channels (for example 5.1) are refused with ErrAudioUnsupported. Opus is checked against the RFC 8251 conformance vectors, not against ffmpeg’s output sample for sample. Vorbis is not decoded: the one pure-Go decoder tried failed the comparison with ffmpeg, and no decoder was written.
data.decode#decode: github.com/go-avkit/decode decodes H.264 and HEVC / H.265 (4:0:0, 4:2:0, 4:2:2 and 4:4:4 at 8 to 16 bits since v0.15.0; 4:2:0 at 8 and 10 bits before) to planar YUV and FLAC, MP3, Opus, since v0.6.0, AAC and, since v0.9.0, linear PCM (WAVE) to PCM, in pure Go with no cgo. Vorbis and MP2 are not decoded. H.264 is decoded by our own h264, whose decoding layer began as oops1/go.264 v1.12.0 (BSD-2-Clause) and which has run the H.264 path since v0.12.0; HEVC, since v0.10.0, by our own h265 v0.22.0 since v0.11.0 (it was gen2brain/h265 up to v0.9.0; that dependency is gone; until v0.14.0 a format a Frame could not carry was refused at the SPS with an ErrUnsupported that names it, and since v0.15.0 only separate colour planes are). Speed is on the history page: v0.10.0’s x86 8-bit slowdown (decode#101) is closed, and no stream is slower than v0.9.0 since v0.11.0. decode is the avkit-facing layer around them and the place where claims are measured. It is the only module in this organisation that produces pictures or sound.
data.edit-lists#Edit lists:
Since v0.5.0, DecodeTrack and PosterFrame apply an MP4 track’s edit list by default, as ffmpeg does: a picture presented before an edit’s media time, or at its end or after, is decoded but not returned, presentation times are shifted so the pictures of the edit start at 0 (or at the length of the empty edit that delays the track), and PosterFrame’s t is a presentation time. This is a change from v0.3.0 for a file whose edit list trims or delays the track. Config.IgnoreEditList (ffmpeg’s -ignore_editlist 1) returns every picture labelled with track time, as v0.3.0 did.
An edit list the package does not apply is refused with ErrEditList rather than guessed at (a media rate other than 1, an edit lasting to the end of the media, an empty edit after the first edit that shows media, a media time before the track). Matroska has no per-track video edit list, so the first picture’s time is now 0, as in ffmpeg. Known divergence: for a fragmented MP4 with a trimmed start, ffmpeg and decode return different pictures (21 against 19 on the fixture), because ffmpeg switches its edit list support off for a fragmented file and decode cannot tell the file is fragmented yet (go-avkit/decode#20).
data.limits#Limits: A stream is untrusted. Config.MaxFrameMBs (default 36864, a 4096x2304 picture) and MaxSampleBytes (default 64 MiB) are checked before anything sized by the stream is allocated. Bomb tests assert a refusal under a memory limit for both video codecs, and the parsers and sample decoders are fuzzed with a committed corpus. AudioConfig limits the channel count, the block size, a coded sample and the PCM a track may return. PosterFrame has bounds of its own in PosterConfig: MaxSamples (default 600) caps the samples decoded for one picture, past it the error is ErrPosterLimit, and MaxTrackSamples (default 1«20) refuses a longer sample list.
data.measured#How it was measured:
Every picture’s MD5 is compared with ffmpeg’s -f framemd5, single thread.
ITU-T H.264.1 conformance suite (AVCv1): 81 streams tried, 73 are claimed. Measured on h264 (whose decoding layer comes from go.264 v1.12.0), 69 give the same pictures as ffmpeg today, as h264’s README also states (69 of its 73 streams); 4 more (MR2 to MR5_TANDBERG) need MMCO 5 and frame_num gaps (oops1/go.264#2) and are skipped until h264 carries the fix. The other 8 are not claimed: 5 interlaced and 3 using FMO/ASO. JCT-VC conformance suite HEVC_v1 (ITU-T H.265.1): 147 streams. 143 give the same pictures as ffmpeg. Three are decided by the suite’s own MD5 because ffmpeg disagrees with it and decode agrees with it (SAODBLK_A_MainConcept_4, SAODBLK_B_MainConcept_4, VPSSPSPPS_A_MainConcept_1). One, TSUNEQBD_A_MAIN10_Technicolor_2 (luma and chroma bit depths differ), is refused by ffmpeg; since v0.15.0 decode decodes it to the suite’s MD5. The bitstreams are not in the repository, so the conformance test runs only when pointed at them. JCT-VC range extensions (since v0.15.0): all 47 streams the test can run decode to the suite’s md5, including Bitdepth_A, Bitdepth_B and TSUNEQBD (10-bit luma, 9-bit chroma). Streams and real files in the repository: 29 H.264 and 5 HEVC streams run in CI against ffmpeg’s MD5s; real MP4 and Matroska files (5 H.264, 7 HEVC) are recorded as hashes.
data.poster-frame#One picture: id, _ := decode.FirstVideoTrack(r) f, err := decode.PosterFrame(r, id, 12.5, decode.PosterConfig{}) PosterFrame (since decode v0.2.0) returns the picture with the greatest presentation time at or before t, the very bytes DecodeTrack returns for it, without decoding the whole track: decoding starts at the last sync sample at or before the picture’s sample and stops as soon as the picture is out. It takes H.264 (avc1, avc3), HEVC (hvc1, hev1), VP8 (vp08) and VP9 (vp09, since v0.16.0; profiles 1 to 3 since v0.17.0); another codec (AV1, …) is refused by name, since v0.9.0, with a *CodecError (codec "vp09" is not supported; errors.Is(err, ErrUnsupported) holds), not reported as a corrupt sample. A negative or NaN t is ErrTime.
data.speed#Speed:
decode is slower than ffmpeg on every video input measured, and that is an open defect (go-avkit/decode#2). Measured on decode v0.3.0, single core, on an Apple M4 Max with ffmpeg 9.0.2 -threads 1, 5 interleaved rounds:
Input decode (fps) ffmpeg (fps) decode / ffmpeg H.264 High 1080p, real clip 36.5 173.1 0.21 HEVC Main 10 2160p, real clip 10.3 27.9 0.37 committed H.264 and HEVC streams 0.21 to 0.41 This table is the v0.3.0 measurement, when HEVC ran on gen2brain/h265; the HEVC speed since v0.10.0 is on the history page. The profiles put the hot spots mostly in the wrapped libraries: the old go.264 wrapper had no arm64 assembly kernels (h264 has them), and gen2brain/h265 took its assembly motion compensation at 8 bits only. The measurement is on arm64; an amd64 one is still needed. The audio decoders are not measured yet.
data.using-it#Using it:
r, _ := container.NewReader(file) frames, err := decode.DecodeTrack(r, trackID, decode.Config{}) for _, f := range frames { // display order use(f.Y, f.Cb, f.Cr, f.YStride, f.CStride, f.Width, f.Height, f.PTS) } Since v0.14.0, decode.Frames is the streaming form of DecodeTrack, for H.264 and HEVC, with the same edit-list and timestamp handling:
for f, err := range decode.Frames(r, trackID, decode.Config{}) { if err != nil { return err } use(f) } It returns an iter.Seq2[*Frame, error]. Each *Frame is a fresh allocation the caller owns, so it can be kept or sent to another goroutine; leaving the loop (break, return) stops the decoding; an error is the last pair, after every picture decoded before it. On the 15 files of the edit-list corpus it yields exactly DecodeTrack’s pictures, and both equal ffmpeg’s md5. A caller that uses each frame and lets it go saves the slice: on Zen 4, one core, Frames against DecodeTrack, H.264 alien 2.63 s to 2.53 s (-4 %) with page faults 194 000 to 25 000, fade 1.05 s to 1.00 s (-5 %), HEVC alien-main 2.66 s to 2.47 s (-7 %).
Since v0.15.0, decode uses h265 v0.24.0 and releases each picture to it once it is converted to a Frame, so the decoder reuses the planes; the output is unchanged. Zen 4, one core, 7 ABBA rounds, median of 14 runs per side, against v0.14.0 (this measures that change alone): alien-main Frames 2.401 s to 2.213 s (-7.8 %), DecodeTrack 2.580 s to 2.444 s (-5.3 %); fade-main Frames 1.358 s to 1.261 s (-7.2 %), DecodeTrack 1.461 s to 1.386 s (-5.1 %); minor page faults per frame on alien-main Frames 1437 to 283. H.264 runs on h264 v0.12.0 (a store-forwarding stall removed), 2.2 to 2.7 % faster on Zen 4: alien 2.561 s to 2.491 s, fade 1.034 s to 1.011 s. Since v0.15.1, decode uses h264 v0.13.0: H.264 decoding is 3.3 to 3.6 % faster on Zen 4 (alien 2.266 s to 2.185 s, fade 0.881 s to 0.852 s, from the h264 notes). Since v0.15.2, it uses h264 v0.14.0: 5.9 % faster on alien (2.207 s to 2.076 s) and 3.5 % on fade (0.849 s to 0.819 s) on Zen 4; ffmpeg 6.1.1 is still faster on H.264, 2.07 times on alien and 2.28 times on fade. Since v0.15.3, it uses h264 v0.15.0 (CABAC residual decoding in one assembly kernel call, output identical to v0.14.0 under a differential fuzz test): alien 2.051 s to 2.025 s (1.3 %) on Zen 4; ffmpeg is about 2.02 times faster on alien (2.025 s against 1.004 s). Since v0.16.1, the SBR filter banks of HE-AAC v2 run in float32 (go-simd/floats v0.33.0): 699 ms to 670 ms (-4.2 %) on a short clip, one Zen 4 core; the PCM is no longer bit identical across CPU routes and is held to stated error bounds instead. Since v0.17.1, the parametric-stereo all-pass plan is driven by tick (go-simd/floats v0.41.0, AllPass3Plan.RunTick): BenchmarkPSDecode/ps 2053 us to 2044 us (-0.45 %, within a noise of about 0.3 %), output unchanged.
H.264 input: an avcC record (decode.NewAVCC) or a TrackConfig (decode.NewTrack) with length-prefixed samples, fed with DecodeSample and ended with Flush; or a raw Annex B stream (decode.New, DecodeAnnexB). HEVC input: the same calls choose HEVC for a track whose sample entry is hvc1 or hev1; decode.NewHVCC takes an hvcC record, decode.NewHEVC takes in-band parameter sets, and DecodeAnnexB a raw .265 stream. Main 10 frames hold little-endian 16-bit samples. Output: frames in display order, with planes, strides, size, chroma format, bit depth and PTS. Behaviour change in v0.15.0: a Frame may now be 4:0:0, 4:2:0, 4:2:2 or 4:4:4, at 8 to 16 bits, with luma and chroma depths that differ. Read Frame.Chroma, BitDepth and BitDepthC rather than assuming 4:2:0: (Frame).SampleBytes(plane) gives the bytes per sample of a plane (1 at 8 bits, otherwise 2, a little-endian 16-bit word) and (Frame).ChromaSize() the size of the chroma planes. A 4:0:0 frame has no Cb or Cr, and its BitDepthC is 0. Frames are bounded by their bytes, computed without overflow, so the same limit applies on every platform (decode#108, a 32-bit overflow, is fixed).
data.what-it-decodes#What it decodes:
VP8 and VP9 run faster when the program is built with GOEXPERIMENT=simd (Go 1.27, amd64 AVX2 or arm64): govpx’s native-SIMD kernels are compiled only then, and a library cannot set it for its importers. On one core that is 2.07x to 4.96x. How to build and the measurements are in the decode README.
Codec and profile State H.264 Constrained Baseline; Baseline without FMO/ASO bit-exact H.264 Main, progressive (CAVLC, CABAC, B pictures, weighted prediction, multiple and long-term references, MMCO) bit-exact H.264 High, 4:2:0 8-bit, progressive bit-exact on the streams measured; no JVT FRExt stream measured yet H.264 interlaced (PAFF, MBAFF), FMO/ASO, Extended refused with ErrUnsupported H.264 High 10, 4:2:2, 4:4:4, lossless refused with ErrUnsupported VP8 since v0.16.0, and VP9 profiles 0 to 3 (4:2:0, 4:2:2, 4:4:4, 8, 10 and 12 bits) since v0.17.0, over thesyncim/govpx v0.5.2 libvpx’s decoder test vectors match on every picture: 373 of 376 (all 62 VP8, 311 of 314 VP9), none differs, with and without GOEXPERIMENT=simd; the test fails on any differing vector VP9 4:4:0 (yuv440 vectors) refused with ErrUnsupported naming 4:4:0 (Frame has no such sampling); 3 of the 376 vectors HEVC Main, Main Still Picture, 4:2:0 8-bit bit-exact against ffmpeg HEVC Main 10, 4:2:0 10-bit bit-exact against ffmpeg HEVC 4:0:0, 4:2:2 and 4:4:4, 8 to 16 bits, luma and chroma depths that differ (since v0.15.0, on by default) the 47 JCT-VC range-extension streams the test can run match the suite’s md5 HEVC 4:4:4 coded as separate colour planes refused with ErrUnsupported HEVC frame of more than 2³¹−1 bytes refused with ErrOverLimit

data.history#History and measurements:
The per-version history and the speed measurements of the modules, moved here from the overview so that page can stay short. The detail of the decoder is also on the decode page.
An audio/video toolkit. It reads and writes MP4/ISO-BMFF, Matroska/WebM and MPEG-TS, reads ADTS, MP3, FLAC, Ogg, WAV and AVI, and moves tracks between them without re-encoding, with their subtitles (WebVTT, SRT, TTML, 3GPP tx3g, and PGS in Matroska), edit lists and metadata. It extracts one audio track as an audio-only file (ADTS, MP3/MP2, FLAC, Ogg, WAV). It carries Apple Lossless (ALAC) and Dolby TrueHD in MP4 and Matroska (not in MPEG-TS), and reads, writes and carries chapters (MP4 chpl and QuickTime chapter track, Matroska Chapters), moved by Cut and Concat. container.Segment (avkit v0.14.0) cuts a file into the initialisation and media segments of an HLS or DASH presentation — CMAF/fMP4 for video and audio, WebVTT documents for subtitles — aligned across tracks at the video keyframes; the playlists and the MPD are written by go-streamkit’s hls and dash packages (streamkit v0.2.0), and the module github.com/go-avkit/avkit/media (v0.2.0) joins the two: media.HLS, media.DASH and media.WriteDir. VOD only, one video track at most: no live, no encoding ladder. Since avkit v0.15.0, container.EncryptSegments encrypts those segments with Common Encryption — cenc (AES-CTR) or cbcs (AES-CBC, 1:9 pattern for video) — from a key the caller supplies, keeping NAL and slice headers clear, and container.Encrypt, Decrypt and DecryptFile work on any fragmented MP4 (ffmpeg decrypts the output). With media.Keys(...) (media v0.2.0), media.HLS, media.DASH and media.WriteDir state how a player gets the key: EXT-X-KEY and EXT-X-SESSION-KEY in the HLS playlists, ContentProtection in the DASH manifest. There is no licence logic and no key server, and the content key itself never enters media. It also reads the H.264, H.265, VP8 and VP9 bitstream syntax. Only decode turns samples into pictures, for H.264 and for HEVC in 4:0:0, 4:2:0, 4:2:2 and 4:4:4 at 8 to 16 bits (4:2:0 at 8 and 10 bits before decode v0.15.0), within the limits that page states. h265 carries a decoder of our own since v0.14.0 and reconstructs inter prediction since v0.15.0: 7147 hashed conformance pictures verified (6638 inter), 0 mismatched; the 3091 pictures of the 59 hashless streams are unverified (h265#48). Since v0.16.0 it has a public Decoder API (Decode and Flush, pictures in output order, typed errors, limits on picture size and memory); v0.14.0 and v0.15.0 could panic on a hostile SPS, fixed in v0.16.0. v0.20.0 is faster than the previous third-party decoder on every stream measured on x86 (1.03 to 1.09 times on 8-bit, 3.07 on Main 10) and still 0.19 to 0.30 of ffmpeg’s speed, an open defect; v0.21.0 adds Unit.Tag, carried to Output.Tag. v0.22.0 decodes 8-bit pictures natively into bytes, with the output unchanged (md5 equal to ffmpeg’s): on one pinned Zen 4 core, against v0.21.0, alien Main 91.1 to 107.6 fps (+18 %), fade Main 82.2 to 95.3 (+16 %), alien8 103.9 to 125.7 (+21 %), Main 10 unchanged; on an Apple M4 (indicative) +1 to +8 %. Behaviour change in v0.22.0: Plane.Pix is renamed Pix16, with no alias, and an 8-bit picture carries Pix8 []uint8 instead (exactly one of the two is non-nil; Is8, At and Len read either). decode v0.11.0 uses it. v0.23.0 decodes the 7 JCT-VC RExt streams that use cabac_bypass_alignment_enabled_flag (all 31 of their picture hashes match) and the base layer of the 9 MV-HEVC conformance streams (md5 of the shipped base-layer YUV on 371 pictures); speed is not re-measured. decode v0.13.0 (h265 v0.23.0) decodes 1 of the 7 streams and 6 are refused (4:4:4 with 16-bit samples, a format a Frame cannot carry), and decodes the MV-HEVC base layer (md5 equal to the shipped _0.yuv). v0.24.0 adds an opt-in reuse of pictures: with Options.RecyclePictures set, a caller that is done with a picture calls (*DecodedPicture).Release() and the decoder reuses its planes once the decoded picture buffer no longer references it. The default is unchanged (every picture is its own allocation, never reused); a picture that is not released is never reused, and releasing twice, or with the option off, does nothing. h265.Decoder alone, one pinned Zen 4 core, option off to on: alien Main 104.2 to 113.9 fps (+9 %), fade Main 93.2 to 101.2 (+8 %), alien Main 10 89.2 to 100.3 (+12 %), alien8 121.1 to 124.9 (+3 %), with 3 to 5 times fewer page faults per frame. The output is unchanged on all 196 JCT-VC conformance streams. Behaviour change in decode v0.15.0: HEVC in 4:0:0, 4:2:2 and 4:4:4, at 8 to 16 bits with luma and chroma depths that may differ, now decodes by default (until v0.14.0 only 4:2:0 at 8 or 10 bits did). A caller must read Frame.Chroma, BitDepth and BitDepthC (SampleBytes(plane) and ChromaSize() help); the 47 JCT-VC range-extension streams the test can run match the suite’s md5. Still refused: separate colour planes, and a frame of more than 2³¹−1 bytes (ErrOverLimit). decode v0.15.0 also uses h265 v0.24.0 (picture reuse, 5 to 8 % faster through Frames and DecodeTrack on Zen 4) and h264 v0.12.0 (2.2 to 2.7 % faster); decode#108, a 32-bit overflow, is fixed. decode v0.15.1 uses h264 v0.13.0: H.264 decoding is 3.3 to 3.6 % faster on Zen 4 (alien 2.266 to 2.185 s, fade 0.881 to 0.852 s, from the h264 notes). decode v0.15.2 uses h264 v0.14.0: 5.9 % faster on alien (2.207 to 2.076 s) and 3.5 % on fade (0.849 to 0.819 s) on Zen 4; ffmpeg is still 2.07 times faster on alien and 2.28 times on fade. decode v0.15.3 uses h264 v0.15.0 (CABAC residual decoding in one assembly kernel call, output identical to v0.14.0): alien 2.051 to 2.025 s (1.3 %) on Zen 4, ffmpeg about 2.02 times faster on alien (2.025 s against 1.004 s). decode v0.16.1 runs the SBR filter banks of HE-AAC v2 in float32: 699 to 670 ms (-4.2 %) on a short clip, one Zen 4 core, 1.59 to 1.52 times ffmpeg. decode v0.17.1 drives the parametric-stereo all-pass plan by tick (go-simd/floats v0.41.0): 2053 to 2044 us (-0.45 %, within a 0.3 % noise) on that benchmark. Measured on 2026-11-25 (Zen 4, one pinned core, load about 1, 9 interleaved rounds, ffmpeg 6.1.1 with one thread): HE-AAC v2 decodes at 1.42 times ffmpeg’s user time (was 1.74 when decode#77 opened); ffmpeg’s real time also holds 209 ms of system time that our in-process benchmark does not pay, so user time is the comparable figure. Behaviour change in v0.19.0: the planes of a picture from Decoder.Output are read-only views, not copies, and Stride can exceed Width; a caller that modifies samples must call Clone() first. Since decode v0.10.0, decode decodes HEVC with h265 (gen2brain/h265 is gone); v0.10.0 was 7 to 12 % slower than v0.9.0 on x86 8-bit streams, and since v0.11.0 no stream is slower than v0.9.0 (Main 10 is 2.5 times faster). Nothing here decodes sound except decode’s FLAC, MP3, Opus and, since decode v0.6.0, AAC-LC and HE-AAC v1 and, since v0.7.0, HE-AAC v2 (full profile since v0.8.0; not Vorbis or MP2).
h265 speed (v0.20.0, from its README): frames per second by CPU time, one core (AMD Ryzen 9 7950X, taskset -c 5, ABBA of five rounds each, load 0.44 to 1.21, 2026-11-16). “Third-party” is gen2brain/h265, the decoder decode v0.9.0 used, measured through DecodeTrack; ffmpeg is 6.1.1 with -threads 1. No parity is claimed: it is far slower than ffmpeg, an open defect.

data.verification#Verification of the bitstre:
Where another implementation can answer the same question, it is asked: the h264 reference picture set against ffmpeg -debug mmco (3110 reference pictures across 101 streams, zero disagreements), its reference lists against an independent pure-Go decoder (785 lists, 18 streams, zero disagreements), and the implicit bi-prediction weights over all 65536 pairs the clause clips to. bitstream, h264, boolcoder, vp8 and vp9 produce no pixels: no residual entropy decoding, transform, motion compensation or deblocking. h265 reconstructs pictures since v0.14.0 (intra) and v0.15.0 (inter, with deblocking and SAO), and decode uses it for HEVC since v0.10.0.
h265 v0.14.0 also changes Unit.TemporalID, which returned TemporalId + 2 up to v0.13.2 and now returns TemporalId. Since v0.14.0 decode.Frames(r, trackID, cfg) streams one picture at a time (an iter.Seq2[*Frame, error], each Frame owned by the caller).

data.module-notes#Module notes:
The landing page gives each module one line; the detail is here.
avkit reads and writes MP4/ISO-BMFF, Matroska/WebM and MPEG-TS; reads ADTS, MP3, FLAC, Ogg, WAV and AVI; extracts an audio track as ADTS, MP3, FLAC, Ogg or WAV. It copies, cuts, joins and concatenates tracks with no re-encoding, carrying WebVTT, SRT, TTML, 3GPP tx3g and PGS subtitles, ALAC and TrueHD audio, chapters, edit lists, encoder priming, metadata and cover art. container.Segment cuts CMAF/fMP4 and WebVTT segments for HLS and DASH (VOD; the playlists are written by go-streamkit), container.EncryptSegments encrypts them with Common Encryption (cenc, cbcs) from a key you supply, and media.Keys states how a player gets the key (EXT-X-KEY and EXT-X-SESSION-KEY in HLS, ContentProtection in DASH). ConformHVC1 makes an HEVC file one macOS will show. Since v0.17.0 a Matroska file that would unlace more frames than a track or the file may hold is refused with ErrReaderLimit before anything is allocated; see hostile files. bitstream: the bit reader with the formats’ Exp-Golomb codes, both NAL framings, and the unescaping a payload is meaningless without. h264: H.264/AVC syntax and the derivations of clause 8.2: parameter sets and slice headers, then picture order counts, the reference picture set, the reference lists and the prediction weights. Since v0.11.0 the decoder runs more of go-videodsp/kernels (AVX2 on amd64) with the API unchanged. Whole decode of 1080p clips, one core, Apple M4 Max (indicative, load 11 to 17): alien 5.75 to 6.05 s down to 2.28 to 2.39 s, fade 2.01 to 2.13 s down to 0.82 to 0.89 s (about 2.5 times faster), framemd5 equal to ffmpeg’s. Still 2.3 to 2.9 times slower than ffmpeg, an open defect; Zen 4 is not re-measured. Later speed steps are on the decode page. h265: the NAL layer, parameter sets, slice segment header and picture boundaries, and since v0.14.0 an HEVC decoder of our own. All 52215 conformance slices walk to their last bit; 509 of 509 hashed intra pictures match their decoded picture hash SEI (v0.14.0); 7147 hashed pictures, 6638 of them inter, 0 mismatched (v0.15.0). Speed and the per-version changes are on the history page. boolcoder: the boolean arithmetic decoder VP8 and VP9 read their compressed partitions with. vp8: the VP8 frame tag and key-frame header, the parts of a frame that are plain bytes and bit fields. vp9: the uncompressed frame header, and the superframe index that packs several frames into one sample. worker (v0.1.2): a js/wasm Web Worker over the container reader and the H.264 decoder. poster returns a JPEG of the frame at a time, probe returns container, codec, size and duration. A request can only lower the worker’s limits, and a hostile file is refused rather than decoded. This table is kept by hand, and it had fallen six modules behind — it listed avkit alone while the organisation held seven. To check it, ask the organisation which of its repositories are Go modules:
for r in $(gh repo list go-avkit --limit 60 --json name --jq '.[].name'); do gh api repos/go-avkit/$r/contents/go.mod --jq '.name' >/dev/null 2>&1 && echo "$r" done | sort
